issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when, after addressing the trial court’s principal reasons and carefully examining the evidence, it justifies a contrary view that is not excluded by the governing limits on appellate review.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after relying on reasons the Supreme Court regarded as flimsy or baseless.
The High Court addressed the relevant reasons for acquittal and re-examined the evidence before reaching a contrary view.

The evidence included eyewitness accounts of the assault, medical findings consistent with the fatal spear injury and the witnesses’ injuries, and evidence concerning the field demarcation and the parties’ dispute.
The Supreme Court concluded that the trial court’s acquittal was perverse and that the High Court had kept within the limits governing appeals against acquittal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to reverse the acquittal, and its exercise of appellate power was proper.
issues.legal_principle: Section 423 of the Code of Criminal Procedure gives an appellate court equal powers in appeals against conviction and acquittal. Those powers remain subject to the presumption of innocence, the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of reasonable doubt, regard for the trial court’s assessment of witnesses, and restraint where the trial court had the advantage of seeing and hearing them. The appellate court must address the principal reasons for acquittal and explain its contrary view; if two views of the evidence are reasonably possible, the acquittal should not be disturbed. The judgment relies on Ram Jag v. State of U.P. for this summary of the principles.

rule.if: state_appeal_from_acquittal and (trial_acquittal_reasons_perverse or trial_acquittal_reasons_fl tous) and appellate_court_addressed_principal_reasons and appellate_court_justified_contrary_view

predicates.state_appeal_from_acquittal: The prosecution challenged an acquittal in an appellate court.
predicates.trial_acquittal_reasons_perverse: The trial court based its acquittal on reasons that were perverse.
predicates.trial_acquittal_reasons_fl tous: The trial court based its acquittal on reasons that were flimsy or baseless.
predicates.appellate_court_addressed_principal_reas: The appellate court examined the principal reasons that had led the trial court to acquit.
predicates.appellate_court_justified_contrary_view: The appellate court carefully examined the evidence and gave reasons supporting a view contrary to the acquittal.

issues.definition: When a prosecution appeal challenges an acquittal and the appellate court addresses the principal reasons for it and justifies a contrary view, reversal may be upheld where the acquittal rested on perverse, flimsy, or baseless reasons.

issues.legal_issue: The convictions of an armed group and the member who inflicted a fatal spear injury were supported by the group’s shared object to assault and the members’ awareness that grievous harm from a sharp weapon was likely.
material_facts: The accused formed an armed group carrying lathis and a spear and shared an object to assault two members of the opposing party.
One member thrust the spear into a victim’s chest, causing his death.
The other members participated in the assault, and the Supreme Court considered that they must have known that grievous harm with a sharp weapon was likely in pursuit of the group’s object.

The High Court convicted the spear-wielder of murder and rioting and convicted the other members of rioting and assault-related offences; the Supreme Court considered those convictions justified and described the treatment of the other members as cautious and lenient.
issues.conclusion: The convictions were justified: the spear-wielder’s murder conviction and the convictions of the other members were upheld, although the other members could have been convicted of grievous hurt committed in prosecution of the common object.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 147, 148 and 149 of the Penal Code, members of an unlawful assembly may be held responsible for offences committed in prosecution of its common object. The Court observed that although the common object was to assault rather than necessarily to murder, the members knew that grievous hurt with a sharp cutting weapon was likely; the other members could therefore have been convicted under Section 326 read with Section 149. The spear-wielder’s direct fatal act supported his conviction under Section 302, while the convictions under Sections 323 read with 149, 147 and 148 were upheld.

rule.if: armed_unlawful_assembly and shared_object_to_assault and member_inflicted_fatal_spear_injury and members_knew_grievous_sharp_weapon_harm_likely

predicates.armed_unlawful_assembly: A group assembled with weapons and acted together.
predicates.shared_object_to_assault: The group shared an object to assault members of another party.
predicates.member_inflicted_fatal_spear_injury: One member inflicted a spear injury that caused the victim’s death.
predicates.members_knew_grievous_sharp_weapon_harm_: The members knew that grievous harm from a sharp weapon was likely to be caused in pursuit of their shared object.

issues.definition: When an armed group shares an object to assault, one member inflicts a fatal spear injury, and the members know that grievous harm from a sharp weapon is likely, the convictions of the group members may be upheld.
